entry: English singer, songwriter, and media personality, dubbed the "Prince of Darkness." He co-founded [[Black Sabbath]] in 1968 as its lead vocalist and was dismissed in 1979 over alcohol and drug problems. His solo career began in 1980 with *Blizzard of Ozz*. He sold more than 100 million albums and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2006 and 2024. With his family he starred in the [[MTV]] reality series *The Osbournes* (2002–2005). He gave his final performance in 2025, at the Back to the Beginning concert in Birmingham, England, after announcing it would be his last due to health issues.

American public broadcaster and non-commercial television network, based in Arlington, Virginia. Founded in 1969 and operating since 1970, PBS is a [[Nonprofit organization|nonprofit organization]] and the most prominent provider of educational programming to public television stations in the United States. Its shows include *Nature*, *Nova*, *Frontline* and *Sesame Street*. It has more than 350 member stations, funded by member dues, pledge drives, corporate sponsorships and donations. In 1973 it broadcast the Senate [[Watergate scandal|Watergate]] proceedings nationwide. Until 2025 it also received funding from the Corporation for Public Broadcasting.

High-speed standard for connecting hardware components inside computers. Developed and maintained by the PCI-SIG, PCI Express (PCIe) is designed to replace older expansion buses such as PCI, PCI-X and AGP. It connects graphics cards, sound cards, [[Wi-Fi]] and [[Ethernet]] adapters, and storage devices such as [[Solid-state drive|solid-state drives]] and [[Hard disk drive|hard disk drives]]. Unlike the shared parallel bus of PCI, PCIe uses point-to-point serial links, and each device uses one or more lanes depending on its data needs. Its bandwidth has roughly doubled about every three years, reaching 128 GT/s in version 7.0 (2025).

File format for presenting documents in a manner independent of [[Application software|application software]], hardware and [[Operating system|operating systems]]. Based on the PostScript language, PDF encapsulates a complete description of a fixed-layout document, including text, fonts, vector graphics and raster images. Adobe developed it in 1993 and made the specification free of charge that year; it was standardized as ISO 32000 in 2008, when control passed to an ISO committee. PDF files may also include annotations, form fields, layers, multimedia, [[Encryption|encryption]] and digital signatures. The format grew out of the Camelot Project, begun by Adobe co-founder John Warnock in 1991.

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, a group of synthetic organofluorine compounds with multiple fluorine atoms attached to an alkyl chain. Their high chemical and thermal stability gives them long environmental lifetimes, earning them the nickname "forever chemicals." Widespread use began in 1938 with [[Polytetrafluoroethylene|Teflon]], and PFAS now appear in waterproof fabric, food packaging, firefighting foam and [[Cosmetics]]. Some are [[Carcinogen|carcinogens]] or endocrine disruptors linked to [[Cancer|cancers]], [[Ulcerative colitis]] and thyroid disease. PFOS and PFOA were listed under the Stockholm Convention in 2009 and 2019. Only a few of the thousands of PFAS compounds have undergone comprehensive biological testing.

General-purpose scripting language geared toward web development. Created by Danish-Canadian programmer Rasmus Lerdorf and released in 1995, PHP was originally an abbreviation of "Personal Home Page" and now stands for the recursive "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor." It usually runs on a web server, where its output, such as generated [[HTML]], forms all or part of an [[HTTP]] response. It can also run from the command line. The standard interpreter, powered by the Zend Engine, is free software under the PHP License, and it has been ported to most web servers and operating systems.

Logarithmic scale for specifying the [[Acid|acidity]] or [[Base (chemistry)|basicity]] of an aqueous solution. pH is the negative base-10 logarithm of hydrogen ion activity. At 25 °C, solutions with a pH below 7 are acidic, those above 7 are basic, and pure water is neutral at 7. The neutral value falls below 7 as temperature rises above 25 °C. The scale is conventionally given as 0 to 14, but very concentrated strong acids can have values below 0, and strong bases can exceed 14. The pH of a solution can be measured with a glass electrode and pH meter or with a color-changing indicator. The concept was introduced in 1909 by Danish chemist Søren Peter Lauritz Sørensen at the Carlsberg Laboratory; the exact original meaning of the letter "p" remains disputed. Measurements are important in [[Chemistry]], [[Agronomy]], medicine and water treatment.

Raster-graphics file format that supports lossless [[Data compression|data compression]]. It was developed in the mid-1990s as a non-patented replacement for [[GIF]], whose LZW compression was patented by Unisys, requiring royalties. PNG supports palette-based images with 24-bit RGB or 32-bit RGBA [[Color|colors]], grayscale images with optional transparency, and full-color RGB or RGBA images. It was designed for transferring images on the [[Internet]], so CMYK color is not supported. The format was published as RFC 2083 in 1997 and as ISO/IEC 15948:2004. Its name was proposed on [[Usenet]] by Oliver Fromme, as a recursive acronym meaning "PING is not GIF."

Battle royale video game published by Krafton and first released for [[Microsoft Windows|Windows]] through [[Steam (service)|Steam]] in 2017. Up to one hundred players parachute onto an island, scavenge weapons and fight until one player or team remains, as a safe area shrinks over time. The game was based on mods by Brendan "PlayerUnknown" Greene and inspired by the Japanese film *Battle Royale* (2000). It has been free-to-play since 2022 and has sold more than 75 million copies on personal computers and consoles. Critics praised its approachability and replayability, and it popularized the battle royale genre. It set seven [[Guinness World Records]].

American showman, businessman, and politician known for promoting hoaxes and for founding a circus with James Anthony Bailey. In [[New York City]] he bought Scudder's American Museum, renamed it after himself, and displayed curiosities such as the Fiji mermaid and General Tom Thumb. In 1850 he promoted the American tour of Jenny Lind, paying her $1,000 per night for 150 nights. His museum added America's first [[Aquarium]]. A Republican, he served two terms in the [[Connecticut]] legislature and was elected mayor of Bridgeport in 1875. The adage "there's a sucker born every minute" is often attributed to him, but no evidence shows he coined it.

Ancient Indian grammarian and linguist whose work codified Classical Sanskrit. His masterwork, the *Aṣṭādhyāyī*, is conventionally taken to mark the start of Classical Sanskrit and is the foundational text of *Vyākaraṇa*, one of the six Vedāṅgas, or auxiliary scholarly disciplines of ancient India. It uses a technical metalanguage of syntax, morphology and lexicon, organized according to a series of meta-rules. European scholars in the 19th century called him the "first descriptive linguist," and his approach influenced [[Ferdinand de Saussure]] and Leonard Bloomfield. He is dated variously to the 6th–5th and 4th centuries BCE, and numismatic evidence has been used to place him in the mid-4th century BCE. Some writers call him a [[Brahmin]], though this is uncertain.

[[Probability]], assuming the null hypothesis is true, of obtaining test results at least as extreme as those observed. The null hypothesis usually states that a parameter, such as a correlation or a difference between means, is zero. A small p-value means such an extreme result would be unlikely under that hypothesis. A result is statistically significant if it allows rejection of the null hypothesis, and smaller p-values are taken as stronger evidence against it. Ronald A. Fisher introduced the measure in the 1920s, and his 1925 book *Statistical Methods for Research Workers* formalized its use. Misinterpretation is widespread. In 2016 the American Statistical Association stated that p-values do not measure the probability that the hypothesis is true or the size of an effect, but a 2019 task force said that properly applied significance tests increase the rigor of conclusions.

Unsolved problem in [[Theoretical computer science|theoretical computer science]]. It asks whether every decision problem whose positive answer can be verified quickly can also be solved quickly, where "quickly" means in polynomial time. The class of problems solvable in polynomial time is P, and the class whose answers can be verified in polynomial time is NP. Most researchers believe P ≠ NP, which would mean some problems are harder to solve than to verify. A proof either way would affect [[Cryptography|cryptography]], [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]], economics and many other fields. The problem was formally stated by Stephen Cook in 1971 and independently by Leonid Levin in 1973, after [[Kurt Gödel]] asked in a 1956 letter to [[John von Neumann]] whether theorem-proving could be done in quadratic or linear time. It is one of the seven [[Millennium Prize Problems]], each carrying a US$1,000,000 prize.

Finnish middle- and long-distance runner known as the "Flying Finn" for his dominance of distance running in the 1920s. Nurmi set 22 official world records at distances from 1,500 metres to 20 kilometres and won nine gold and three silver medals in the [[Olympic Games]]. In 1923 he became the first runner to hold simultaneous world records in the mile, the 5,000 m and the 10,000 m. At the 1924 [[Paris]] Olympics he won five gold medals. He was suspended before the 1932 Games over questions about his amateur status, and he retired in 1934. He later coached runners, worked in business and became one of the richest people in [[Finland]]. In 1952 he lit the Olympic flame at the [[Helsinki]] Games, and he is credited with popularizing the "even pace" strategy in running.

Catalan cellist, conductor, and composer, best known for recordings of [[Johann Sebastian Bach|Bach]]'s Cello Suites. Born in El Vendrell, Spain, he found the suites at age 13 and practiced them for 13 years before performing them in public. After Republican Spain fell to the Nationalist forces of [[Francisco Franco]] in 1939, he went into self-exile and refused to return until democracy was restored. He lived in Prades, France, until 1956 and then in Ceiba, Puerto Rico. [[John F. Kennedy]] awarded him the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1963. In 1971 he conducted his *Hymn to the United Nations* at the UN, where he received the U.N. Peace Medal.

Colombian drug lord who founded the [[Medellín Cartel]], which controlled much of the [[Cocaine]] trade into the [[United States]] in the 1980s and early 1990s. Raised in [[Medellín]], Escobar moved from petty crime to working for smugglers in the early 1970s. He founded the cartel in 1976 and established smuggling routes from Peru, Bolivia and Ecuador through Colombia. At his peak he was estimated to have a net worth of US$30 billion, earning him the nickname "King of Cocaine." He was elected an alternate member of the Chamber of Representatives in 1982, but his political ambitions were thwarted by the Colombian and US governments. His cartel was linked to bombings and to murders of police officers, judges and politicians. He was killed by police in his hometown, and the cartel collapsed. Many Colombians regarded him as a "Robin Hood-like" figure, and over 25,000 people attended his funeral.

Chilean poet, diplomat, and politician who won the 1971 [[Nobel Prize]] in Literature. His work ranged from the love poems of *Twenty Love Poems and a Song of Despair* (1924) to surrealist, historical, and political verse. He served as a senator for the Chilean Communist Party. After the government outlawed [[Communism|communism]] in 1948, he fled to Argentina and did not return to Chile for more than three years. He was a close adviser to President [[Salvador Allende]] and later served as ambassador to France. He died in Santiago after the coup led by [[Augusto Pinochet]] overthrew Allende's government. The official cause was prostate cancer, but a 2023 toxicology report found *Clostridium botulinum* in his teeth, and an official inquiry was reopened in 2024. [[Gabriel García Márquez]] called him "the greatest poet of the 20th century in any language."

Maze arcade video game released by Namco in 1980, originally titled Puck Man in Japan. The player eats dots in an enclosed maze while avoiding four colored ghosts, each with its own [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]]. Eating large "Power Pellets" makes the ghosts vulnerable for a time. Designer Toru Iwatani wanted a game that would appeal to women as well as men. The game spawned sequels, merchandise, two television series and the hit single "Pac-Man Fever." The character became Namco's official [[Mascot|mascot]]. The game has generated more than $14 billion in revenue (as of 2016) and sold 43 million units.

Ninth Sapa Inca, who transformed the chiefdom of [[Cusco]] into the [[Inca Empire]] and reigned from about 1438 to 1471. He succeeded his father, Viracocha Inca, after the Chanka–Inca War. His conquests extended Inca rule from the Cusco valley to the [[Lake Titicaca]] basin, the eastern Andean slopes and the [[Quito]] basin. Most archaeologists believe that [[Machu Picchu]] was built as an estate for him. According to the chronicler Garcilaso de la Vega, he created the Inti Raymi festival to celebrate the new year. Some anthropologists regard him as one of the first historical Inca emperors; others see him as a mythological figure marking the start of imperial expansion.

Mechanical game originating in Japan, used as an arcade game and, far more often, for [[Gambling|gambling]]. It fills a niche similar to that of the [[Slot machine|slot machine]] in the Western world. Parlors, which usually also have slot machines, look much like [[Casino|casinos]]. Gambling for cash is illegal in Japan, but players can exchange balls for prize tokens that can be sold for cash off the premises. In 1994 the market was valued at ¥30 trillion. [[Yakuza]] groups long infiltrated the industry, though police crackdowns reduced this from the 1990s. The number of parlors peaked at 18,244 in 1997 and had fallen to 7,665 by 2022.

Cross-and-circle board game from India. Its origins are disputed: some scholars link it to the "Pasha" game described in the [[Mahabharata]], though the descriptions do not clearly match, while others place its development in medieval India. The name derives from the Hindi *paccīs*, "twenty-five," the largest score from throws of cowrie shells. Two to four players move pieces around a cross-shaped board, and the team that moves all its pieces to the finish first wins. The Mughal emperor [[Akbar]] reportedly played it on courtyard boards using human pieces. In 1938 the American company Transogram introduced a board version, Pa-Chiz-Si. Related commercial games include Parcheesi and Ludo.

Series of mountain ranges along the West Coast of [[North America]], from [[Alaska]] to northern and central Mexico. They are part of the North American Cordillera and include the Coast Mountains, Olympic Mountains, Cascade Range and California Coast Ranges. The Insular Mountains of [[Vancouver Island]] lie farther west. In Alaska the ranges contain record-setting tidewater glaciers, while along the coasts of [[British Columbia]] and Alaska the mountains meet the sea in [[Fjord|fjords]] and thousands of islands. In winter, cool air masses from the [[Gulf of Alaska]] bring heavy rain and snow to the ranges north of San Francisco Bay, especially to their western slopes. Plate tectonics shaped the ranges, and the San Andreas fault system in California produces ongoing earthquakes.

Bi-national geographic and cultural region of western North America, also called Cascadia. Its most common conception includes the U.S. states of [[Oregon]], [[Washington (state)|Washington]] and [[Idaho]], and the Canadian province of [[British Columbia]]. Its boundaries are not official, and broader definitions reach into [[Yukon]] and [[Alaska]]. Its largest metropolitan areas are Greater [[Seattle]] (4 million people), Metro Vancouver (3.4 million) and Greater [[Portland, Oregon|Portland]] (2.5 million). The culture is shaped by the Canada–United States border, which was established when most of the region's inhabitants were Indigenous peoples. Historian Ken Coates argued that "the region's history and character have been determined by the boundary."

Theater of [[World War II]] fought between the [[Empire of Japan]] and the Allies in East and Southeast Asia, the Pacific and Indian Oceans, and Oceania. Japan's war with China, the [[Second Sino-Japanese War]], began in 1937, but the Pacific War is more widely dated from 1941, when the United States and United Kingdom entered. On December 7–8, 1941, Japan attacked Pearl Harbor and launched campaigns against the Philippines, Guam, Malaya, Singapore and Hong Kong. The [[Battle of Midway]] in June 1942 is considered a key turning point, and Allied island-hopping campaigns followed, beginning with Guadalcanal and New Guinea. After heavy losses at the [[Battle of Leyte Gulf]], Japanese forces resorted to kamikaze attacks. After the atomic bombings of [[Hiroshima]] and [[Nagasaki]] and the Soviet invasion of Manchuria, Japan surrendered on August 15, 1945.

Philosophy opposing war or violence. The word was coined by French peace campaigner Émile Arnaud and adopted at the Universal Peace Congress in [[Glasgow]] in 1901. A related term, *ahimsa* ("to do no harm"), is central to [[Hinduism]], [[Buddhism]] and [[Jainism]]. In modern times, interest was revived by [[Leo Tolstoy]] in his late works. [[Mahatma Gandhi]] practiced nonviolent resistance, which he called *satyagraha*, in the Indian independence movement, and its example inspired [[Martin Luther King Jr.]] and others in the civil rights movement. Principled pacifists hold that violence is morally wrong, while pragmatic pacifists argue that the costs of war must be avoided. Some pacifists accept force in self-defense. Critics argue that unilateral restraint can enable aggressors.
